analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workers' right to unionize, strike, and bargain, with tougher penalties for employers who retaliate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate vote: introduced with 46 Democratic and independent cosponsors, it sat in the Senate labor committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it easier for workers to form unions and harder for employers to block them. It would tighten the definitions of who counts as an employee and employer, ban mandatory anti-union meetings, let unions collect fees from all workers they represent even in states that ban it, allow sympathy strikes, require binding arbitration when a first contract stalls, and raise penalties for employers who fire or retaliate against strikers. The Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize unions and bargain would gain the most: faster elections, interim protections against pay cuts, reinstatement and damages if fired for striking, double back pay plus punitive damages for retaliation, and a binding arbitration path when an employer refuses to agree to a first contract. Unions would also gain, through permission to collect representation fees in all states, voter-list requirements for elections, and expanded secondary strike rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers trying to organize and unions

how_it_helps.text: It makes firing or permanently replacing a striker an unfair labor practice, and lets interim pay cuts be challenged, so workers can strike without losing their jobs [S3].
It requires union representation elections to be scheduled within roughly 20 business days and lets elections be conducted by mail or electronically, away from employer-controlled locations [S3].
It removes employers' standing to participate in representation proceedings and requires them to hand over worker contact lists to the union seeking an election [S3].
It bans mandatory anti-union campaign meetings and bars employers from forcing workers to sign away the right to join class or collective lawsuits [S3].

It raises civil penalties for violations to as much as $50,000 per violation, doubled to $100,000 for repeat offenders, makes directors and officers personally liable, and lets workers sue in court for damages including punitive damages [S3].

If bargaining for a first contract stalls, a three-member arbitration panel, with one member chosen by the union, one by the employer, and one neutral, would set a binding contract for two years [S3].
It would let collective bargaining agreements require all covered workers to pay fees for representation, overriding state right-to-work laws [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially large ones with nonunion workforces, would bear the cost: higher exposure to lawsuits and penalties, mandatory arbitration of first contracts, tighter joint-employer liability, and reclassification of many independent contractors as employees. Gig-economy platforms and delivery and rideshare companies whose business models rest on contractor classification would face the biggest structural change.

drawbacks.text: Binding arbitration of first contracts takes the outcome out of the parties' hands: if no deal is reached, a government-appointed panel can impose wage and benefit terms for two years based on factors including workers' cost of living and the employer's finances, which critics said overrides genuine negotiation [S3].

The bill's new definition of employee (free from control, outside the usual course of the business, and customarily in an independent trade) would reclassify many independent contractors as employees, which opponents argued would strip gig workers and freelancers of the scheduling flexibility they choose [S3].

The broad joint-employer definition counts indirect or reserved control over working conditions, extending bargaining obligations up supply chains to franchisors and brand companies that do not directly employ the workers [S3].
Allowing unions to collect fees from all represented workers notwithstanding state law would override right-to-work laws in more than half the states [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers in nonunion workplaces, the bill offered substantially stronger legal protection than current law, where violations often carry little penalty and cases can take years. The costs fall mainly on employers, which supporters consider the point; the genuine trade-offs are for independent contractors who may be reclassified against their preference, and for parties in stalled negotiations who would have terms imposed by an arbitration panel rather than agreed by both sides. On balance the design is coherent and favors workers decisively.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, and that committee never voted to send it to the floor; other committees held hearings but the full Senate never considered it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on February 24, 2021, joined by 45 other senators including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer [S1,S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, and no further committee action was recorded on the bill itself [S5].
All 46 cosponsors were Democrats or independents: 44 of the 48 Senate Democrats and both independents [S4].
The Small Business Committee held a hearing on the bill in March 2022 and the Banking Committee held one in June 2022, but the labor committee with jurisdiction never reported the bill [S5].

The House passed its companion bill, H.R. 842, 225-206 on March 9, 2021, with nearly all Democrats in favor and nearly all Republicans opposed, but the Senate never took it up (widely reported; not in the provided sources).
The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023 with the bill having received no floor vote in either chamber's version [S1,S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced union organizing campaigns, higher penalties, and binding first-contract arbitration came out ahead, because the rules stayed as they were. Workers and unions that backed the bill gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers kept the status quo; workers gained nothing

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 45 Senate cosponsors; as chair of the labor committee with jurisdiction over it, never brought it to a committee vote.

for.name: 44 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of nearly the entire Democratic caucus.

for.name: AFL-CIO and organized labor
for.role: Labor union federation and affiliated unions
for.what_they_did: Championed the bill as their top legislative priority and pushed Senate Democrats to pass it.

against.name: Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: Publicly announced he could not vote for the bill, denying Democrats the 50-vote base needed even to attempt floor action.

against.name: Kyrsten Sinema
against.what_they_did: Did not support the bill, joining Manchin in blocking the arithmetic needed for Senate passage.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill unanimously; not a single Republican sponsored or cosponsored it, and the 60-vote threshold for ending debate made their opposition decisive.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business coalitions
against.what_they_did: Ran a major campaign against the bill, urging senators to oppose it.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent, no Republican supported it, and the House companion bill passed 225-206 on a nearly party-line vote.

industries.note: Would face mandatory arbitration of first contracts, secondary strikes, and penalties up to $100,000 per violation for retaliation against organizing workers. Their interest in keeping the status quo runs directly against workers seeking union representation.

The bill's three-part test would reclassify most gig drivers and many freelancers as employees, converting contractors into covered workers. Platforms argue workers lose flexibility; workers would gain minimum protections and bargaining rights.

Would gain mandatory fee collection even in right-to-work states, employer-provided voter lists, faster elections, and sympathy strike rights, strengthening unions as institutions as well as the workers they represent.

A joint-employer definition counting indirect or reserved control would make brand companies and intermediary firms liable for, and party to bargaining over, conditions at workplaces they do not directly employ.
